title: A hotspot phosphorylation site on SHP2 drives oncoprotein activation and drug resistance

paper_content.abstract:
SHP2 is a phosphatase and a critical mediator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)-driven
RAS/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling. Despite promising preclinical data,
SHP2 inhibitors have shown minimal clinical efficacy, with no defined clinical mechanisms of
primary resistance. Here, we elucidate phosphorylation of SHP2 at tyrosine 62 (pY62) as a
hotspot phosphorylation site in the proteome and RTK-driven tumor types in patients. We
demonstrate that SRC family kinases directly phosphorylate SHP2 at Y62, downstream of but not
directly phosphorylated by RTKs. Using biochemical and biophysical analyses, we show that
SHP2Y62D enforces an open, active conformation, resulting in constitutive phosphatase activation
that is sufficient to activate MAPK signaling and confer resistance to allosteric SHP2 inhibitors.
These findings establish that SHP2 pY62 is a phosphorylation hotspot phenocopying mutational
activation, a mechanism of primary resistance to SHP2 inhibitors, and a cancer drug target distinct
from wildtype SHP2.
paper_content.introduction:
SHP2, encoded by the PTPN11 gene, is a non-receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase1-5 that
serves as a critical mediator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling to the RAS/MAPK
pathway6,7. In its basal state, SHP2 adopts an autoinhibited closed conformation, in which the N-
terminal Src homology 2 (SH2) domain occludes the protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) domain
active site8,9 (Fig. 1a). Upon activation of RTKs, SHP2 binds to phosphotyrosine-containing motifs
through its SH2 domains, relieving autoinhibition and enabling its catalytic activity. In addition to
its phosphatase function, SHP2 acts as a signaling scaffold, integrating RTK inputs and facilitating
the activation of downstream effectors such as RAS and ERK10-15.

Activating mutations in SHP2 have been well characterized as oncogenic drivers in hematologic
malignancies, including juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) and subsets of acute myeloid
leukemia (AML), and as germline mutations which underlie Noonan syndrome (NS)16. More
recently, SHP2 has emerged as an essential signaling node in RTK-driven solid tumors, where
SHP2 is rarely mutated17-19. Functional genetic studies have demonstrated that SHP2 is required
for survival in RTK-driven cancer models, including those driven by oncogenic epidermal growth
factor receptor (EGFR), anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), and fibroblast growth factor receptor
(FGFR) alterations20. These findings catalyzed the development of allosteric SHP2 inhibitors
(SHP2i) that function as molecular glues, stabilizing the autoinhibited conformation of the protein
(e.g., SHP099, RMC4550, TNO155)21. Although these agents have demonstrated potent
preclinical activity, clinical trials to date have reported negligible objective response rates (ORR =
~0%)22-24 with stable disease at best, and have been associated with dose-limiting toxicities,
including fatigue, rash, and cytopenias. These challenges highlight the need to investigate
mechanisms of primary resistance to SHP2i and identify biomarkers that modulate SHP2
dependence and therapeutic response.

Considerable preclinical effort has gone into uncovering genetic resistance mechanisms to SHP2i
including activating SHP2 mutations that lock the protein in an open, active state, making it
resistant to allosteric inhibitors designed to bind the inactive form. However, activating mutations
are rare in RTK-driven solid tumors. Additionally, much attention has focused on phosphorylation
of SHP2 at its canonical C-terminal tyrosines, Y542 and Y580, which are known to promote
scaffolding interactions and downstream signaling15,25-27, but their direct effect on SHP2’s catalytic
activity remains unclear28.

Despite the clinical momentum behind SHP2 inhibitors, emerging evidence points to alternative
phosphorylation sites, including SHP2 Y62 (pY62) as potential modulators of inhibitor sensitivity.
pY62 was initially discovered in cytokine-stimulated hematopoietic stem cells29. More recently,
pY62 was found to be enriched in SHP099 resistant FLT3-driven acute myeloid leukemia cells
and was associated with SHP099 resistance possibly through enforcing an open, active
conformation of SHP230. Whether SHP2 pY62 occurs broadly across cancer types—and in which
biological contexts this modification meaningfully alters signaling, protein biochemistry, and
structure—remains incomplete.

Our interest in SHP2 pY62 was driven by two independent observations that underscore its
potential significance. First, a comprehensive phosphoproteomic analysis identified SHP2 pY62
as one of the most recurrent phosphorylation events in the human proteome. Second, SHP2 pY62
is one of the most differentially enriched phosphopeptides across multiple RTK-driven tumor types
in patient samples. This set of observations in normal cells and tissues, cancer cells, and patient
samples prompted us to investigate the functional, mechanistic, and therapeutic consequences
of SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation.

Here we show that SHP2 pY62 is conserved across cell and cancer types and that SRC family
kinases directly phosphorylate SHP2 at Y62, downstream of RTKs. We also show that SHP2Y62D
enforces an open, active conformation, resulting in constitutive phosphatase activation that is
sufficient to activate MAPK signaling and confer resistance to allosteric SHP2 inhibitors.
paper_content.results:
SHP2 pY62 is a hotspot phosphorylation in normal cells/tissues and cancer cells and is
enriched in diverse RTK-driven tumor types

Inspired by cancer genomics efforts to define frequent “mutational hotspots”31-33, we performed a
comprehensive analysis of the human phosphoproteome using PhosphositePlus34. We identified
239,530 human proteins phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) across normal cells and tissues,
and cancer cells (Fig. 1b) (Supplementary Data 1 ). We determined the reported frequency of
every phosphosite by computing the sum of MS_LIT, the number of published studies reporting
the phosphosite, and MS_CST, the number of unpublished mass spectrometry experiments
performed and curated by Cell Signaling Technology, on PhosphoSitePlus. We posited that the
most frequent phosphosites may be enriched for functionality, and focused analysis on the top
2400 (1%) of phosphosites. In line with this assertion, many of the most frequent phosphosites
were known kinase activation loop sites including GSK3α pY279, GSK3β pY216, and ERK2
pY187 (Supplementary Data 1). We examined proteins with multiple phosphorylation sites and
found that the top differentially phosphorylated protein was not a kinase, but the protein
phosphatase SHP2 (Fig. 1c). The known SHP2 C-terminal tyrosine phosphosites Y542 and Y580
(pY542, pY580) (Fig. 1a) were abundant, but surprisingly, the most abundant SHP2 phosphosite
was the tyrosine Y62 (pY62) (Fig. 1c).

We next determined the experimental characterization frequency by comparing LT_LIT, the
number of low-throughput (LT), experimentally validated studies in PhosphositePlus
(Supplementary Data 1), with MS_LIT + MS_CST. By this metric, SHP2 pY62 was reported far
less frequently than the canonical C-terminal phosphorylation sites pY542 and pY58034 (Fig. 1d).
Despite this underrepresentation, SHP2 Y62 is evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates, down
to Xenopus (Supplementary Fig. 1). Notably, SHP2 Y62 is not conserved in the closely related
human phosphatase SHP1, where it aligns with phenylalanine 60 (F60), a non-phosphorylatable
residue. In contrast, the adjacent SHP2 Y63 is conserved and aligns with SHP1 Y61, indicating
selective evolutionary retention of the neighboring tyrosine, rather than the Y62-equivalent site.
SHP2 Y62 is located in a structured core on a loop between the βD and βE strands of the SHP2
N-terminal SH2 (nSH2) domain8. Among the 110 SH2-domain containing proteins in humans,
Y62-homologous tyrosines are present in 12 proteins, some of which are frequently
phosphorylated (Supplementary Fig. 1)35.

Protein phosphorylation can differ between cancer cell lines and tumors36. To understand the role
of SHP2 pY62 in patients, we determined its abundance and enrichment across genomically
defined human tumor types based on publicly available data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor
Analysis Consortium (CPTAC)37 and National Omics Data Encyclopedia (NODE)38. SHP2 pY62
has been reported as the single most differentially increased phosphosite in patients with EGFR-
mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), compared to their wild-type (WT) counterparts39
(Fig. 1e). In fact, SHP2 pY62 was more increased than phosphorylated EGFR itself (Fig. 1e,
Supplementary Data 2). Additionally, SHP2 pY62 was the second most differentially increased
phosphosite in patients with FGFR2-altered cholangiocarcinoma40 (Fig. 1f), and differentially
increased in CPTAC datasets in patients with EGFR-amplified head and neck squamous cell
carcinoma41, EGFRvIII-positive glioblastoma42, and EGFR-altered high grade glioma43, compared
to WT counterparts. In contrast, SHP2 pY62 was one of the most significantly decreased
phosphosites in KRAS-mutant NSCLC relative to wild-type NSCLC39 (Fig. 1g, Supplementary
Data 2). Our identification of SHP2 pY62 as one of the most frequently detected phosphosites in
the human phosphoproteome, along with its evolutionary conservation and selective retention
across orthologs and SH2 domains, and its high frequency in RTK-driven patient tumor types
suggests that Y62 phosphorylation may exert distinct conformational or functional effects that
contribute to RTK-driven oncogenesis.

SHP2 pY62 is downstream of RTKs, but Y62 is not phosphorylated by RTKs

Given the high abundance of pY62 across RTK-driven tumors, we hypothesized that RTKs signal
to and directly phosphorylate SHP2 Y62 in cells (Fig. 2a). To test this hypothesis, we developed
a phosphospecific SHP2 pY62 antibody and validated it in SHP2 knock out (KO) cells
overexpressing SHP2 and the phosphodead mutant Y62F (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). We serum-
starved U-2 OS (osteosarcoma) and BT20 (EGFR-amplified triple-negative breast cancer) cells
and exposed them to various RTK ligands (EGF, FGF1, PDGF). RTK stimulation led to RTK
phosphorylation at 5-10 minutes, with eventual detection of SHP2 pY62 much later, suggesting
SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation is downstream of RTKs (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Fig. 2c-e). However,
when we exposed RTK stimulated cells to RTK inhibitors against EGFR, FGFR, and PDGFR in
serum starved media, there was no decrease in SHP2 pY62 (Fig. 2c), showing that SHP2 Y62 is
not directly phosphorylated by RTKs.

SRC family kinases (SFKs) phosphorylate SHP2 Y62, Y542, and Y580

To determine the direct kinase for SHP2 Y62, we leveraged The Kinase Library, a recently
developed global atlas of protein kinome in vitro substrate specificities44,45, based on the peptide
primary sequence surrounding the phosphosite (Supplementary Data 3). For SHP2 pY62, RTKs
were predicted as the top candidate kinases (Fig. 3a). JAK3, a non-RTK, was also highly
predicted. However, exposure of cells to the JAK3 inhibitor tofacitinib did not alter the level of
SHP2 pY62 (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Interestingly, non-RTKs, such as SRC family kinases
(SFKs) SRC, YES1, and FYN, were in the bottom quartile with lower confidence scores. Since
inhibiting RTKs did not alter the SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation, we wanted to test if SFKs can
phosphorylate SHP2 Y62.

To test this hypothesis, we first used pharmacologic methods (Fig. 3b). Dasatinib is a multi-kinase
inhibitor that targets not only SFKs but also ABL, PDGFR, and c-KIT46 (Fig. 3b). Treatment with
dasatinib readily decreased SHP2 pY62 levels in U-2 OS cells (Fig. 3c) and HCC827 cells (EGFR-
mutant NSCLC) (Fig. 3d). Dasatinib treatment also decreased SHP2 pY542 and pY580 levels in
U-2 OS cells (Fig. 3c) but only pY542 in HCC827 cells (Fig. 3d). Since dasatinib has a wide range
of targets including SFKs, ABL, and c-KIT, we next chose the selective SFK inhibitor SU665647
which inhibits SRC, YES1, FYN, and LYN; asciminib48 which binds to the myristoyl binding pocket
and inhibits ABL; and ripretinib49, which inhibits c-KIT, to narrow down candidate kinases (Fig.
3b). Treatment of U-2 OS cells with SU6656 decreased SHP2 pY62, pY542, and pY580 but there
was no change in SHP2 phosphorylation with SU6656 in HCC827 cells (Fig. 3d). Treatment with
asciminib or ripretinib did not change SHP2 phosphorylation levels (Supplementary Fig. 3b).

The SFKs comprises 8 human kinases50, three of which–-SRC, YES1, and FYN–-are ubiquitously
expressed in all tissues. In contrast, other SFK kinases (BLK, FGR, HCK, LCK, and LYN) are
expressed in specific tissue types51. To our knowledge, there are no SFK inhibitors selective to
individual SFKs. To better deconvolute the contributions of specific SFK kinases, we tested the
SFK inhibitors saracatinib52 (SRC and ABL inhibitor), CH695375553 (YES1 inhibitor), and PP254
(FYN and LCK inhibitor) (Fig. 3b) which are more selective than dasatinib or SU6656 but less
potent. In HCC827 cells, SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation was inhibited by saracatinib, CH6953755
and PP2, and Y542 phosphorylation was altered by PP2 and saracatinib at high concentrations,
but not Y580 phosphorylation (Fig. 3e). In U-2 OS cells, SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation was inhibited
by saracatinib only at high concentrations, while Y542 and Y580 phosphorylation were inhibited
by saracatinib even at 1 µM (Supplementary Fig. 3c), but not by CH6953755 (Supplementary Fig.
3d) or PP2 (Supplementary Fig. 3e).

We further investigated the cell-type specificity of SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation. Since 1) dasatinib
decreased SHP2 pY62 levels in HCC827 and U-2 OS cells, 2) inhibitors of the non-SFK kinase
targets of dasatinib did not decrease SHP2 phosphorylation, and 3) selective SFK inhibitors
inhibited SHP2 pY62 levels in HCC827 but not in U-2 OS cells, we hypothesized that SHP2 Y62
phosphorylation is maintained by distinct SFK family members in a context-dependent manner,
and that broad SFK inhibition is required to suppress SHP2 pY62 across diverse cell types.

To test this hypothesis, we tested double and triple combinations of the SFK selective inhibitors
saracatinib, CH6953755, and PP2 in HCC827 and U-2 OS cells. Combining two drugs reduced
SHP2 pY62, pY542, and pY580 levels more than single drugs, and combining all three drugs
reduced levels more than combining two drugs (Fig. 3f, Supplementary Fig. 3f).

We also used mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from the SYF knock out mouse (SRC-/-, YES1
-/-, FYN -/-)55 as a genetic tool to test the hypothesis that SFKs phosphorylate SHP2 pY62. We
found that SHP2 pY62, pY542, and pY580 levels were inhibited compared to WT MEFs (Fig. 3g).
Thus, pharmacologic inhibition and genetic loss of the SFKs SRC, YES1, and FYN reduce SHP2
phosphorylation at Y62, Y542, and Y580.

Our initial growth factor experiments showed that SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation is downstream of
RTKs (Fig. 2b). We used our pharmacologic and genetic models to situate SFKs in RTK-SHP2
signaling. EGF-dependent SHP2 phosphorylation at Y62, Y542, and Y580 was abrogated when
U-2 OS cells were pretreated with dasatinib or SU6656 (Supplementary Fig. 3g). EGF-, FGF1-,
and PDGDF-dependent SHP2 phosphorylation at Y62 was abrogated in our SYF KO MEF models
compared to WT MEFs (Supplementary Fig. 3h-j). In contrast, SHP2 Y542 and Y580
phosphorylation were abrogated in SYF KO MEFs under FGF1 stimulation but not under EGF or
PDGF stimulation (Supplementary Fig. 3h-j).

Finally, to further validate that SFKs phosphorylate SHP2 Y62, we performed in vitro kinase
assays using bacterially purified recombinant SHP2. SRC, YES1, and FYN kinases
phosphorylated SHP2 WT at Y62 but not the Y62F phosphodead mutant (Fig. 3h). SRC, YES1,
and FYN also phosphorylated Y542 and Y580 in vitro (Fig. 3h). Together these data show that
SHP2 Y62 is a direct substrate of SFKs, and that SHP2 Y542 and Y580 can also be
phosphorylated by SFKs.

SHP2 Y62 phosphomimetic protein constitutively increases phosphatase activity

SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation has been proposed to disrupt its autoinhibited state through the
introduction of negative charge at the N-SH2/PTP interface, thereby enhancing phosphatase
activity, and this has been supported by biochemical and cellular experiments with the Y62
phosphomimetic mutants30,56,57. We corroborated these prior results by conducting Michaelis-
Menten enzyme kinetics with the Y62D mutant, which showed a 2.4-fold increase in k /K when
cat m
compared with wild-type SHP2 (Fig. 4a). Tyrosine to aspartate mutation is commonly used as a
phosphomimetic to model the effects of phosphorylation, though it may not fully recapitulate the
structural or binding consequences of a bona fide phosphotyrosine at this site. By contrast, the
Y542 and Y580 phosphorylation sites are thought to mediate intramolecular interactions with the
SHP2 SH2 domains or mediate intermolecular interactions with other SH2-containing proteins.
SH2-mediated interactions with tyrosine-phosphorylation proteins cannot be readily mimicked
using D/E substitutions, and indeed, the Y542D and Y580D mutations did not significantly impact
SHP2 activity (Fig. 4a). Furthermore, the combination of Y542D or Y580D with Y62D did not
appreciably impact the gain-of-function effect of Y62D (Fig. 4a).

When SHP2 auto-inhibition is disrupted by mutations, it becomes less responsive to activation by
phosphopeptides58. Indeed, unlike wild-type SHP2, Y62D-containing SHP2 variants could not be
activated by binding to an IRS-1-derived phosphopeptide (Fig. 4b). To further examine whether
these mutations disrupt auto-inhibition, we used differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF)
(Supplementary Fig. 4). Previous studies have shown that SHP2 variants with disrupted
autoinhibition tend to have lower melting temperatures59. Indeed, only SHP2 variants containing
the Y62D mutation, but not Y542D or Y580D, had decreased melting temperatures (Fig. 4c).
Collectively, these experiments show that the Y62D mutation disrupts SHP2 auto-inhibition and
corroborates the assertion that Y62 phosphorylation may disrupt auto-inhibition through
electrostatic effects.

SHP2 Y62D samples mixed open and closed conformations through increased exchange
in its buried nSH2 domain

Since the SHP2Y62D phosphomimetic protein exhibited increased enzymatic activity (Fig. 4a) and
decreased thermal instability (Fig. 4c), and since SHP2 oncogenic mutation propensity for an
open conformation correlates with increased catalysis and increased dynamic and solvent
exposure60,61, we hypothesized that SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation increases catalysis by enforcing
an open, dynamic conformation. We investigated this hypothesis using computational, structural,
and biophysical methods. We used AlphaFold2 to analyze conformational changes in SHP2Y62D
(Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Data 4) and compared the predicted structure to crystal
structures of SHP2WT, which adopts a closed conformation (PDB: 2SHP)8, and SHP2E76K, the only
SHP2 mutant with a crystal structure resolved in an open conformation (PDB: 6CRF)58. While
AlphaFold2 is not specifically powered for optimal structural prediction of missense mutations,
nonetheless, SHP2 Y62D was predicted to have a 22 Å root mean square deviation (RMSD) when
aligned with the WT crystal structure, but a 1.1 Å RMSD when aligned with the SHP2E76K structure
oncogenic mutant crystal structure, suggesting an open confirmation (Fig. 5a). We crystallized
the SHP2Y62D mutant and solved its structure at 2.63 Å resolution (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Table
1). The Y62D crystal structure exhibited a closed conformation, with a 0.5 Å RMSD when aligned
with the SHP2WT crystal structure (Fig. 5b).

Given the discordance between our biochemical and computational data and compared to our
structural data, we hypothesized that SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation samples both the closed and
open state conformations. To investigate the conformational state of the SHP2Y62D mutant, we
performed hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) with recently developed
peptide disambiguation and analysis tools62 comparing SHP2Y62D to SHP2WT and the SHP2
phosphomimetic mutant Y542D/Y580D. Compared to WT, SHP2Y62D exhibited increased
deuterium uptake across peptides spanning not only the nSH2 domain (where Y62 is located),
but also in the PTP domain mediated by amino acids that bind to and maintain nSH2 domain
autoinhibitory interactions (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. 6). Notably this PTP domain peptide
region (496-510) also includes S502, G503, and Q506 which bind to the nSH2 domain, are known
cancer-associated mutations61, and activate SHP2 in deep mutational scanning studies63. This
pattern is consistent with increased destabilization of the closed, autoinhibited conformation and
adoption of an open conformation relative to SHP2WT. In contrast, the Y542D/Y580D mutant
showed minimal differences in hydrogen exchange relative to WT, indicating that these
phosphomimetic substitutions do not strongly alter the conformational ensemble (Supplementary
Fig. 6). Together, these data demonstrate that the Y62D mutation promotes an open, active-like
conformation of SHP2, distinct from WT and Y542D/Y580D.

SHP2 Y62 phosphomimetic mutation activates MAPK signaling and causes resistance to
SHP2 inhibitors

Since SHP2 pY62 is enriched in RTK-driven tumors, we tested the role of SHP2 Y62
phosphorylation in cancer cells. We knocked out endogenous PTPN11/SHP2 using CRISPR-
Cas9 in BT20 and U-2 OS cells, which are frequently used to model SHP2 alterations30,58
(Supplementary Fig. 2a), and complemented this with lentiviral overexpression of SHP2WT,
aspartate and phenylalanine mutants at Y62 and Y542/Y580. Complementation with empty vector
control was not tolerated by cells, consistent with PTPN11/SHP2 loss being synthetic lethal in
RTK-driven cancer cells20. SHP2Y62D, but not SHP2Y62F, sustained maximal MAPK signaling as
measured by phosphorylated MEK (pMEK) and phosphorylated ERK (pERK) in SHP2 KO BT20
cells, suggesting that SHP2 pY62 is necessary for maximal MAPK signaling (Fig. 6a). To
delineate how upstream SFKs modulate MAPK signaling, we used our SYF KO MEF models.
SYF KO showed decreased pMEK and pERK as compared to WT MEFs (Fig. 3g).

Given the abundance of SHP2 pY62 across cancer cells and tumors, and the minimal response
rates conferred by SHP2i in the clinic, we hypothesized that SHP2 pY62 confers resistance to
SHP2i. We performed biochemical inhibition assays using purified recombinant SHP2WT and
SHP2Y62D proteins. SHP099 IC values were 0.2319 μM for WT and 1.356 μM for Y62D
50
(Supplementary Fig. 7), a statistically significant shift. These data show that the Y62D variant has
reduced sensitivity to allosteric SHP2 inhibition. We tested varied allosteric SHP2 inhibitors
including SHP099, RMC4550, and TNO155, which are based on similar scaffolds that stabilize
the SHP2 autoinhibited conformation20,64,65. SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation as modeled by SHP2Y62D
resulted in resistance to SHP099, RMC4550, and TNO155, as measured by sustained pERK
signaling, as well increased GAB1 phosphorylation which is a direct readout of SHP2 scaffolding
function66 (Fig. 6b-d).

Data reproducibility statement
To ensure the rigor and reproducibility of our findings, all experimental procedures were
conducted following standardized protocols with appropriate controls. Detailed methods, including
reagent sources, catalog numbers, and RRIDs, are provided to enable exact replication. All
experiments were conducted with at least three biological replicates, and statistical analyses were
performed in accordance with established guidelines.

In silico analysis of pY62 abundance
Phosphorylation_site_dataset.gz was obtained from PhosphoSitePlus34. MS_LIT (the number of
published studies reporting the phosphosite) was added to MS_CST (the number of unpublished
mass spectrometry experiments performed by Cell Signaling Technology reporting the
phosphosite) to obtain the number of observations in Fig. 1b and c. LT_LIT (the number of low
throughput, experimentally validated publications supporting the site) was divided by the total
number of observations [(LT_LIT+1)/(MS_CST+MS_LIT)] to obtain the ratio of literature support
and abundance of phosphopeptide observation in Fig. 1d.

The phosphosite abundance in KRAS mutations vs WT tumors and EGFR mutations vs WT
tumors in lung adenocarcinoma was obtained from Gillette et al (2020) – Supplementary table
S4 and S4M39. The phosphosite abundance in FGFR altered vs non-altered tumors in
intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma was obtained from Dong et al (2022)40. We analyzed relative log
fold-changes within each dataset, without normalization to total protein levels and plotted with
GraphPad (Prism, RRID:SCR_002798). We used published phosphoproteomic summary
statistics and focused on relative ranking of phosphosite enrichment within each dataset;
therefore, no new hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-comparison adjustments
were performed.

SHP2 inhibitors treatment with EGF stimulation, the cells were serum starved for 24 hours and
treated with allosteric SHP2 inhibitors for an hour and followed by 10 minutes EGF stimulation

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Karunaraj, P., Scheele, R., et al. characterized biochemical and structural properties of the SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation using
the Y62D phosphomimetic mutant. The authors’ bioinformatics study attempted to substantiate the importance of the Y62
phosphorylation. Using various kinase inhibitors, the authors identified SRC and other SFKs as the kinases that directly
phosphorylate SHP2 at Y62.
I appreciate that the authors employed multidisciplinary approaches to convey their point. However, there is insufficient
evidence for SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation by SRC and other SFKs, as the authors claim. This is because the inhibitor studies
presented (Fig. 2, 3, and Supplemental Fig. 3) lack essential data; none of these blots display the amount of the inhibitor-
targeted kinases. For example, the authors should include a blot showing depletion of active pY1068 EGFR with erlotinib
treatment, alongside pY62 SHP2 (Fig. 2c). All the authors’ inhibitor studies suffer from the same problem. The authors must
show that the added inhibitors had the intended effect on targeted kinases (decrease/disappearance of the active
RTKs/SFKs) along with the level of SHP2 phosphorylation.
Also, where is the experimental evidence for pY62 being a drug-resistant mutation? Was there a previous study determining
IC50 for the pY62 mutant against SHP2 inhibitors? If not, the authors should determine IC50 against one representative
SHP2 inhibitor to make the title of this manuscript valid.
The authors presented Fig.6 as evidence for pY62 drug resistance. This suffers from the same issue as Figs. 2 and 3 as
stated above. Fig.6B-D does not show phospho-EGFR level with EGF and the level of SHP2 after the transfection. What
happened to the level of SHP2 with each inhibitor?
Other points are the following:
Figure 1B-1G: The content of these figures is not clear at all.
Fig.1B and 1C: What does the Y-axis of the graph correspond to? I understand that the authors identified a total of 239,531
phosphosites in all human proteins combined, but why are there multiple hits at y-axis (hits) = 1? Do these correspond to
proteins with 1 phospho-sites? But, that doesn’t make sense since I see a lot of points above 100 hits. In summary, what
does the “hit” correspond to? The authors must describe this point clearly in the manuscript.
Fig.1C and 1D:
Line 107-110: These statements appear to be contradictory. According to the authors, SHP2 pY62 is the most abundant in
the database search, but pY62 is less reported than the canonical pY542 and pY580. Please provide a proper explanation
on this point.
Fig.1E-1G: The authors found pY62 SHP2 as the most abundant phosphorylation in different cancer cell lines except for
KRAS-mutant NSCLC. Considering tyrosine phosphorylation comprises only ~ < 1-2 % of the entire proteome at most, the
authors’ finding is pretty shocking. Also, the phosphorylation abundance of different studies cannot be compared since
different sample preparation methods, LC, as well as mass spectrometry settings, are variable and influence the determined
abundance (or amount) of phosphopeptides.
If the authors wish to highlight the significance of pY62, a previous study (ref 30) seems to be the most suitable for
elaboration, instead of the Figure 1 results.
As to Reference 30, this study found that FLT3 phosphorylates SHP2 at Y62, as opposed to the authors’ finding. Please
elaborate on this point.
Figures 2 and 3: As stated on the first page, the level of inhibitor-targeted kinases should be shown on blots. Also, Fig.3a is
difficult to see.
Figure 4B: This is probably the most interesting result in this manuscript. The Y62D mutant becomes insensitive to the
presence of an allosteric peptide activator, while the peptide can activate the other mutants. Where is the peptide binding
site?
Figure 5A: Structural alignment between an AlphaFold predicted model and a crystal structure of SHIP2 in a closed
conformation (top right).
• The figure does not appear to make sense. The PTP domain appears very similar in both structures, with the only
difference being the orientation of the SH2 domain. Did AlphaFold provide alternative structures that closely resemble the
closed conformation?
Figure 5C: The percent exchange structure map
The preparation of the fully-deuterated standard poses an issue. The point of doing a fully-deuterated experiment is to obtain
the maximum deuterium uptake of each peptide under the same labeling strength (pH, temperature, and deuterium dilution
factor) as that of the labeling experiment. This allows us to normalize the deuterium uptake of each peptide and
express them as the percent exchange. This is important since the structural flexibility of different regions in the same state can be
compared. For example, the structural flexibility of region A and region B in the same protein (state) can be compared since
a fully-deuterated experiment corrects for the back-exchange difference between the two regions (corrects for back-
exchange dependence on amino acid composition/sequence of peptides). It also enables the comparison of the percent
exchange between different proteins, provided that the fully-deuterated experiments are appropriately performed.
The labeling strength is highly dependent on labeling temperature. So, the authors’ result vastly underestimates structural
flexibility due to the higher temperature employed for the full-deuterated experiment. For example, consider the following
scenario where you are analyzing a 10-residue peptide. The maximum possible uptake is 9 (no proline), and you want to
determine the fully-denatured/deuterated uptake of this peptide. The labeling strength is lower at 15 °C than at 37 °C. So, the
experimentally determined maximum uptake of all peptides will be higher at 37 °C (Say Duptake = 7 for this peptide) than at
15 °C (Duptake = 5). If you then determine the same peptide uptake to be 3, the calculated percent exchange at 37 °C and
15 °C is 43% and 60%, respectively. A viable remedy for this issue is to correct the deuterium uptake data using the different
temperature factor (or repeat the fully-deuterated experiments).
Alternatively, since Fig.5C uptake plots (in Da, the same peptide uptake comparisons) are appropriate, I suggest that the
authors keep these exchange uptake data. It will be helpful if the authors indicate/highlight peptide regions in the SHP2
structure more clearly.
Also, based on the HDX-MS results, can the authors speculate how the pY62 mutant (Y62D) confers drug resistance? Is the
Y62D mutant drug resistant like the pY62 mutant?
In summary, the title of this manuscript does not align with the content. The manuscript requires major revision, with a
substantial number of additional experiments needed to show a connection between pY62 activation and drug resistance.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper reports a thorough exploration of phosphorylation of SHP2 on Y62 as a molecular mechanism of sustaining
SHP2 in an active form and as a mechanism of resistance to SHP2 inhibition. The data generally support the conclusions
drawn by the authors. Overall, the work will be a meaningful contribution to the field, and I am supportive of publication after
the refinement of the x-ray structure is completed (see below) and the authors make the requisite textual edits to give the
prior work proper recognition.
Major points:
1) The authors unnecessarily downplay the prior identification of pY62 that was reported in two other manuscripts. They do
cite both papers, but their text in the introduction and discussion minimizes the value of the earlier work and makes it appear
as if the authors are making a breakthrough discovery of Y62 phosphorylation. They should be more forthright in
acknowledging the prior work documenting Y62 phosphorylation as a resistance mechanism. What makes this work stand
out is that it more fully explores the generality of Y62 phosphorylation across cancer cell types and the scope of contexts in
which the modification may impact signaling, reports a pY62 phosphoselective Ab to probe direct versus indirect induction of
the pY mark, thereby assigning phosphorylation to SFKs, rather than the RTKs, and uses Y62D as a phosphomimetic for
structural analysis, HX-MS, and biochemical studies to complement the cellular work.
2) Review of the x-ray structure table, text, pdb validation report, model, and map shows that the claim in the table of 2.63 Å
resolution is not congruent with the text, which states a resolution of 2.9 Å, and that the data set is not complete, particularly
in the outermost shell. The Rwork and Rfree values are unexpectedly high, even for the claimed 2.9 Å resolution, and the
quality of the map and model fit could be substantially improved. Attention to the refinement might also clarify whether there
could be a bridging H2O molecule between D61 and D62.
One other minor point - the enzymatic data to measure catalytic parameters appear to substantially overestimate the activity
of the WT (unmutated) protein compared to values published elsewhere. The basal activity of wt SHP2 is difficult to measure
accurately, but it is not clear why that would be true.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
SHP2 is a phosphatase and a critical mediator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)-driven RAS/mitogen-activated protein
kinase (MAPK) signaling. Despite promising preclinical data, SHP2 inhibitors have shown minimal clinical efficacy, with no
defined clinical mechanisms of primary resistance. Therefore, it is important to elucidate the underlying mechanism on the
lack of clinical response of SHP2 inhibitors in human cancer and to develop new therapeutic strategies to target SHP2.
In this study, the authors elucidated phosphorylation of SHP2 at tyrosine 62 (pY62) as a hotspot phosphorylation site in the
proteome and RTK-driven tumor types in patients. They demonstrated that SRC family kinases directly phosphorylate SHP2
at Y62, downstream of but not directly phosphorylated by RTKs. Using biochemical and biophysical analyses, the authors
showed that SHP2 Y62D (a phosphor tyrosine mimic) enforces an open, active conformation, resulting in constitutive
phosphatase activation that is sufficient to activate MAPK signaling and confer resistance to allosteric SHP2 inhibitors. Their
findings establish that SHP2 pY62 is a phosphorylation hotspot phenocopying mutational activation, a mechanism of
primary resistance to SHP2 inhibitors, and a cancer drug target distinct from wildtype SHP2.
This study employed a number of complementary approaches and the experiments were well done. The conclusion was
solid and well justified. The manuscript was well written and easy to follow. This study answered an urgent and important
question for the SHP2 filed and provided novel therapeutic approaches to target active SHP2, instead of inactive SHP2. It is
recommended that the study be published in Nature Communications.

phosphorylation of SHP2.

pY62. This observation is fully consistent with our model: we likewise find that SHP2 pY62
increases with RTK activation, but our biochemical, kinase, and inhibitor data indicate that the
phosphorylation event is mediated by SFKs rather than by the RTKs themselves.

becomes insensitive to the presence of an allosteric peptide activator, while the peptide can
activate the other mutants. Where is the peptide binding site?
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. SHP2-activating phosphopeptides bind the
canonical pY-binding cleft of the nSH2 (high-affinity) and cSH2 (low-affinity) domains (Eck,
Nature 1996). We are not aware of any crystal structures of human SHP2 nSH2 bound to pIRS1
(Y1172), which was the peptide used in our experiments (characterized in Fujimoto, JBC 1994).
Structures of Syp (mouse SHP2) nSH2 bound to pIRS1 (Y895) and pPDGFR (Y1009) as well

interactions stabilize the open, active conformation by relieving nSH2-mediated autoinhibition.
Y62, however, is not part of the peptide-binding surface. It lies instead at the nSH2-PTP
interface, where phosphorylation—or the Y62D phosphomimetic—destabilizes autoinhibition
and constitutively favors the open state. As a result, Y62D is already “activated” and cannot be
further stimulated by the pIRS1 peptide, whereas other mutants retain an autoinhibited ground
state that the peptide can still unlock.
Thus, the peptide binds the established nSH2 interface, while Y62D activates SHP2 through a
distinct structural mechanism that renders it insensitive to additional allosteric activation.
• Figure 5A: Structural alignment between an AlphaFold predicted model and a crystal
structure of SHIP2 in a closed conformation (top right). The figure does not appear to make

closely resemble the closed conformation?
We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. In Figure 5A, the structures were
superimposed on the PTP domain because the defining conformational difference between
open and closed SHP2 states is the position of the SH2 domains; the PTP domain itself remains
largely unchanged. Because Y62D introduces a single substitution within the nSH2 domain,
close alignment of the PTP domains between the AlphaFold-predicted and experimentally
solved structures is expected and consistent with known SHP2 conformational behavior.
Regarding alternative conformations, AlphaFold2 did generate multiple models for SHP2 Y62D.
As shown in the revised Supplementary Figure 5, the top 4 ranked models adopt open
conformations, whereas the 5th ranked model more closely resembles the closed state. These
outputs are in agreement with our HDX-MS and crystallographic data demonstrating that SHP2
Y62D can sample both conformations but preferentially occupies the open conformation. All
relevant AlphaFold models have now been included in Supplementary Figure 5.
Supplementary Figure 5
• Figure 5C: The percent exchange structure map
The preparation of the fully-deuterated standard poses an issue. The point of doing a fully-
deuterated experiment is to obtain the maximum deuterium uptake of each peptide under
the same labeling strength (pH, temperature, and deuterium dilution factor) as that of the
labeling experiment. This allows us to normalize the deuterium uptake of each peptide and
express them as the percent exchange. This is important since the structural flexibility of
different regions in the same state can be compared. For example, the structural flexibility of
region A and region B in the same protein (state) can be compared since a fully-deuterated
experiment corrects for the back-exchange difference between the two regions (corrects for
back-exchange dependence on amino acid composition/sequence of peptides). It also
enables the comparison of the percent exchange between different proteins, provided that
the fully-deuterated experiments are appropriately performed.
In our HDX/MS workflow, which follows standard practice in the field, the fully deuterated control
is used to determine the maximum possible deuterium uptake for each peptide. To obtain this,
we fully unfold the protein, deuterate it, and measure the resulting mass of each peptide. These
values allow us to correct all forward-exchange data for D-to-H back-exchange, which occurs
during chromatographic processing. In our hands, back-exchange is typically 10-40%, and we
exclude peptides with excessive back-exchange (>50%) to maintain high confidence.
After this correction, deuterium uptake can be compared within the same peptide across
conditions (e.g., WT vs mutant). However, as the reviewer notes, back-exchange correction
alone does not make peptides with different amino-acid compositions directly comparable,
because each sequence has its own intrinsic exchange rates that cannot be precisely
normalized on a residue-by-residue basis. For this reason, percent exchange should not be
compared across peptides of different sequences, but comparisons among identical peptides
(e.g., WT vs point mutants) are valid and appropriate.
• The labeling strength is highly dependent on labeling temperature. So, the authors’ result
vastly underestimates structural flexibility due to the higher temperature employed for the
full-deuterated experiment. For example, consider the following scenario where you are
analyzing a 10-residue peptide. The maximum possible uptake is 9 (no proline), and you
want to determine the fully-denatured/deuterated uptake of this peptide. The labeling
strength is lower at 15 °C than at 37 °C. So, the experimentally determined maximum
uptake of all peptides will be higher at 37 °C (Say Duptake = 7 for this peptide) than at 15 °C
(Duptake = 5). If you then determine the same peptide uptake to be 3, the calculated
percent exchange at 37 °C and 15 °C is 43% and 60%, respectively. A viable remedy for
this issue is to correct the deuterium uptake data using the different temperature factor (or
repeat the fully-deuterated experiments).
We thank the reviewer for raising this point and appreciate the opportunity to clarify the purpose
of the full-D control in our HDX-MS experiments. We appreciate the reviewer’s broader point
that labeling conditions influence absolute percent-exchange values. The full-D control serves a
distinct purpose from the forward-exchange reaction and is not intended to replicate its
conditions. Its sole purpose is to provide an accurate estimate of back-exchange so that
deuterium-uptake curves for each peptide can be properly corrected.
To achieve complete deuteration, the protein must be fully unfolded, which we accomplish by
increasing the temperature before quenching. This ensures that all exchangeable amides are
maximally exposed and allows us to determine the true upper limit of deuterium incorporation.
Because this step is designed to measure back-exchange after quenching, rather than any
property of the forward-exchange reaction, the full-D sample does not need to match the
temperature or folding state of the time-point samples prior to the quench.
If the full-D control were performed under the same folded-protein conditions as the time-point
samples, many residues would remain incompletely exchanged even after 48 hours, leading to
an inaccurate estimate of back-exchange. For this reason, it is standard practice to use
unfolded conditions for the full-D control to ensure complete deuteration and accurate peptide-
level correction.
• Alternatively, since Fig.5C uptake plots (in Da, the same peptide uptake comparisons) are
appropriate, I suggest that the authors keep these exchange uptake data. It will be helpful if
the authors indicate/highlight peptide regions in the SHP2 structure more clearly.
We agree that the uptake plots in Fig. 5C are appropriate for comparing identical peptides
across matched proteins, and we have retained these data in the revised manuscript. To
improve clarity, as suggested, we have now indicated the N- and C-terminal positions of the four
peptides directly on the SHP2 structural model and have revised Figure 5C accordingly. All
peptides analyzed are clearly annotated in the Supplemental Information.
Revised Figure 5c
• Also, based on the HDX-MS results, can the authors speculate how the pY62 mutant
(Y62D) confers drug resistance? Is the Y62D mutant drug-resistant like the pY62 mutant?
SHP099 and related allosteric inhibitors act as molecular glues that bind at the nSH2-PTP
interface and stabilize the autoinhibited, closed conformation of SHP2. Our HDX-MS data show
that the Y62D phosphomimetic shifts the conformational equilibrium toward a more open state,
reducing the stability of this autoinhibited interface. This provides a mechanistic basis for
reduced inhibitor sensitivity: because the closed conformation is less populated, the SHP099
binding interface is correspondingly less accessible.
Consistent with this model, the biochemical inhibition assays in Supplementary Figure 7
demonstrate that SHP2 Y62D exhibits decreased sensitivity to SHP099 compared with wild-type
SHP2, indicating that the phosphomimetic is drug-resistant at the protein level.
In summary, the title of this manuscript does not align with the content. The manuscript requires
major revision, with a substantial number of additional experiments needed to show a
connection between pY62 activation and drug resistance.
We have now performed the additional experiments requested throughout the review—including
direct biochemical measurements of inhibitor sensitivity for SHP2 Y62D, on-target validation of
kinase-inhibitor treatments, and expanded structural and HDX-MS analyses. Together, these
new experiments strengthen the mechanistic linkage between pY62 activation and reduced
sensitivity to allosteric SHP2 inhibition and bring the title and conclusions of the manuscript into
full alignment with the expanded experimental evidence.
We appreciate the Reviewer for these favorable comments.
Major points:
• The authors unnecessarily downplay the prior identification of pY62 that was reported in two
other manuscripts. They do cite both papers, but their text in the introduction and discussion
minimizes the value of the earlier work and makes it appear as if the authors are making a
breakthrough discovery of Y62 phosphorylation. They should be more forthright in
acknowledging the prior work documenting Y62 phosphorylation as a resistance
mechanism. What makes this work stand out is that it more fully explores the generality of
Y62 phosphorylation across cancer cell types and the scope of contexts in which the

identifying SHP2 pY62 in cytokine-stimulated hematopoietic cells and in FLT3-driven AML
models with acquired SHP099 resistance. Our intent was not to minimize these findings, and we
have revised the Introduction and Discussion to acknowledge this work more directly and
prominently.
Specifically, we now state in the Introduction that pY62 was first observed in cytokine-stimulated
hematopoietic stem cells (Louria-Hayon, PNAS 2013) and that pY62 was later found to be
enriched in SHP099 resistant FLT3-driven acute myeloid leukemia cells and was associated
with SHP-099 resistance possibly through enforcing an open, active conformation of SHP2
(Pfeiffer, Cancer Res 2022). In the Discussion, we explicitly note that pY62 has been linked to
SHP2 inhibitor resistance in leukemia and place our work in this context—emphasizing that our
study extends these observations by defining the broader prevalence of pY62 across cancer
types, demonstrating SFK-mediated phosphorylation using a phosphospecific antibody, and
integrating structural, biochemical, and HDX-MS analyses using the Y62D phosphomimetic.
• Review of the x-ray structure table, text, pdb validation report, model, and map shows that
the claim in the table of 2.63 Å resolution is not congruent with the text, which states a
resolution of 2.9 Å.., 
We apologize for this inconsistency. We have corrected the reported resolution in the text from
2.9 Å to 2.63 Å, which now matches the data processing and refinement statistics presented in
the table.
• and that the data set is not complete, particularly in the outermost shell.
We agree that the dataset shows reduced completeness in the highest-resolution shell, and this
is a direct consequence of the anisotropic diffraction that we observed across all SHP2 crystals
collected for this project. We attempted to improve the quality of the crystals through
optimization of both the crystallization and cryo-protection conditions, but the quality of the
crystals did not improve significantly.
To ensure that all useful reflections were used during refinement the data were processed with
STARANISO (Global Phasing). STARANISO applies an anisotropic cutoff limit to include
reflections from strongly diffracting regions of reciprocal space and exclude reflections from
weakly diffracting regions of reciprocal space. The inclusion of the strong reflections during
refinement improves the accuracy of the model and the interpretability of the electron density
maps, while the exclusion of the weak reflections reduces the amount of noise in the electron
density maps. While the use of an anisotropic cutoff limit results in an apparently reduced data
completeness, this is only through the exclusion of reflections that would not improve the
accuracy of the model or the quality of the electron density maps.
• The Rwork and Rfree values are unexpectedly high, even for the claimed 2.9 Å resolution,
and the quality of the map and model fit could be substantially improved.
We agree that the Rwork and Rfree values are higher than typically expected at this resolution,
which is a recognized consequence of refining against an anisotropic dataset. Nevertheless, the
electron-density maps are sufficiently interpretable to support the key conclusion we draw from
the structure—namely, that SHP2 does not adopt an open conformation in this crystal form.
Because our structural interpretation relies on the absence of features consistent with the open
state rather than on modeling fine details of an activated conformation, the quality of the maps is
adequate for this purpose.
• Attention to the refinement might also clarify whether there could be a bridging H2O
molecule between D61 and D62.
There are two waters in the close vicinity of Asp61 and Asp62 (in chain A, W/117 and W/144).
We have included a figure here where the electron density around those two residues is
depicted alongside the final coordinates (rmsd 1.0 sigma, the depicted chain is chain A).
From the attached image it becomes clear that the two waters and the carboxy groups of Asp61
and Asp62 form a trapezoid. However, the distances between the waters and the carboxy
groups are too high to build a water network by themselves. There are no indications in the
electron density that further water molecules are bound close to Asp61 or Asp62.
Figure: Electron density of Asp61 and Asp62 (in purple) including surrounding (5 Å) residues.
Protein in green, the two water molecules are depicted as red spheres and the distance to
Asp61/Asp62 is shown.
• One other minor point - the enzymatic data to measure catalytic parameters appear to
substantially overestimate the activity of the WT (unmutated) protein compared to values
published elsewhere. The basal activity of wt SHP2 is difficult to measure accurately, but it is
not clear why that would be true.
In revisiting our analysis, we realized that the initial activity values had not been normalized
using a standard calibration curve, which can lead to overestimation of absolute catalytic rates.
We have now reprocessed the data using an appropriate standard curve, and the revised
values—shown in Figure 4A—are consistent with published basal activities reported for WT
SHP2. We apologize for this error and thank the reviewer for drawing attention to this point.
We agree that accurately determining the basal activity SHP2, which is an intrinsically
autoinhibited phosphatase, is inherently challenging particularly at very low substrate turnover.
Although additional measurements at lower DiFMUP concentrations could further refine these
estimates, the revised kinetic parameters now fall within the expected range and align with
previously reported values.
We appreciate the reviewer’s comments about our findings.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I thank the authors for taking considerable time to address my concerns. I would also like to commend them for performing through experiments and for providing a clear and thoughtful rebuttal to my comments.
I would like to offer one additional point regarding HDX-MS analysis. Comparison of percent deuterium exchange across different peptides is appropriate provided that fully deuterated control experiments are performed. In response, the authors state that
“back-exchange correction alone does not make peptides with different amino-acid compositions directly comparable,because each sequence has its own intrinsic exchange rates that cannot be precisely normalized on a residue-by-residue basis.”
However, the purpose of back-exchange correction is precisely to normalize for sequence-dependent effect, including intrinsic exchange arising from amino acid composition. Indeed, examination of back-exchange values across peptides often reveal clear sequenced dependence – for example, histidine-containing peptides typically show higher back exchange – demonstrating that such correction explicitly account for intrinsic sequence effects. Once normalized using fully deuterated controls, percent deuterium exchange therefore allows meaningful comparison between different peptides.
If percent exchange across peptides were fundamentally invalid, the utility of back-exchange correction would be unclear. In that case, analysis would be restricted to absolute deuterium uptake (Da), limiting comparisons to identical peptides across conditions and substantially reducing the interpretive power of HDX-MS.
Furthermore, full deuteration can be reliably achieved for most soluble proteins within 1-3 minutes at 25 C using high denaturant concentration (e.g., 6 M guanidine-DCl, or 8 M urea-d4), provided that the labeling strength is sufficient (~20-fold deuterium dilution). I recommend the authors to visit: https://hx2.med.upenn.edu/download.html, which calculates theoretical intrinsic exchange as well as exchange rates in various conditions (pH, temp). Although the site only calculates these rates for given peptide sequences, it may be useful to estimate full exchange times.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors adequately addressed my comments about the referencing of prior work, their X-ray data, and the catalytic activity of the autoinhibited WT enzyme. I defer to the first reviewer regarding comments about SFKs as the kinases responsible for Y62 phosphoryation, as well as their other concerns.

In our HDX-MS workflow, fully deuterated controls were performed for all peptides and used to
correct for D-to-H back-exchange, with peptides exhibiting excessive back-exchange excluded.
This enables robust peptide-level normalization and supports valid comparison of deuterium

To make this analytical choice explicit, we have added the following sentence to the Methods
section: “Fully deuterated controls were used for peptide-level back-exchange correction;
although percent-exchange comparisons across different peptides are feasible in principle, all
analyses here are confined to comparisons of identical peptide sequences across matched
protein variants.”
We believe this clarification addresses the reviewer’s point while accurately reflecting both
standard HDX-MS practice and the analytical framework used in this work.
We appreciate the reviewer’s comments.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

SHP2 is a phosphatase and a critical mediator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)-driven
RAS/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling. Despite promising preclinical data,
SHP2 inhibitors have shown minimal clinical efficacy, with no defined clinical mechanisms of
primary resistance. Here, we elucidate phosphorylation of SHP2 at tyrosine 62 (pY62) as a
hotspot phosphorylation site in the proteome and RTK-driven tumor types in patients. We
demonstrate that SRC family kinases directly phosphorylate SHP2 at Y62, downstream of but not
directly phosphorylated by RTKs. Using biochemical and biophysical analyses, we show that
SHP2Y62D enforces an open, active conformation, resulting in constitutive phosphatase activation
that is sufficient to activate MAPK signaling and confer resistance to allosteric SHP2 inhibitors.
These findings establish that SHP2 pY62 is a phosphorylation hotspot phenocopying mutational
activation, a mechanism of primary resistance to SHP2 inhibitors, and a cancer drug target distinct
from wildtype SHP2.

---

## Introduction

SHP2, encoded by the PTPN11 gene, is a non-receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase1-5 that
serves as a critical mediator of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling to the RAS/MAPK
pathway6,7. In its basal state, SHP2 adopts an autoinhibited closed conformation, in which the N-
terminal Src homology 2 (SH2) domain occludes the protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) domain
active site8,9 (Fig. 1a). Upon activation of RTKs, SHP2 binds to phosphotyrosine-containing motifs
through its SH2 domains, relieving autoinhibition and enabling its catalytic activity. In addition to
its phosphatase function, SHP2 acts as a signaling scaffold, integrating RTK inputs and facilitating
the activation of downstream effectors such as RAS and ERK10-15.

Activating mutations in SHP2 have been well characterized as oncogenic drivers in hematologic
malignancies, including juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) and subsets of acute myeloid
leukemia (AML), and as germline mutations which underlie Noonan syndrome (NS)16. More
recently, SHP2 has emerged as an essential signaling node in RTK-driven solid tumors, where
SHP2 is rarely mutated17-19. Functional genetic studies have demonstrated that SHP2 is required
for survival in RTK-driven cancer models, including those driven by oncogenic epidermal growth
factor receptor (EGFR), anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), and fibroblast growth factor receptor
(FGFR) alterations20. These findings catalyzed the development of allosteric SHP2 inhibitors
(SHP2i) that function as molecular glues, stabilizing the autoinhibited conformation of the protein
(e.g., SHP099, RMC4550, TNO155)21. Although these agents have demonstrated potent
preclinical activity, clinical trials to date have reported negligible objective response rates (ORR =
~0%)22-24 with stable disease at best, and have been associated with dose-limiting toxicities,
including fatigue, rash, and cytopenias. These challenges highlight the need to investigate
mechanisms of primary resistance to SHP2i and identify biomarkers that modulate SHP2
dependence and therapeutic response.

Considerable preclinical effort has gone into uncovering genetic resistance mechanisms to SHP2i
including activating SHP2 mutations that lock the protein in an open, active state, making it
resistant to allosteric inhibitors designed to bind the inactive form. However, activating mutations
are rare in RTK-driven solid tumors. Additionally, much attention has focused on phosphorylation
of SHP2 at its canonical C-terminal tyrosines, Y542 and Y580, which are known to promote
scaffolding interactions and downstream signaling15,25-27, but their direct effect on SHP2’s catalytic
activity remains unclear28.

Despite the clinical momentum behind SHP2 inhibitors, emerging evidence points to alternative
phosphorylation sites, including SHP2 Y62 (pY62) as potential modulators of inhibitor sensitivity.
pY62 was initially discovered in cytokine-stimulated hematopoietic stem cells29. More recently,
pY62 was found to be enriched in SHP099 resistant FLT3-driven acute myeloid leukemia cells
and was associated with SHP099 resistance possibly through enforcing an open, active
conformation of SHP230. Whether SHP2 pY62 occurs broadly across cancer types—and in which
biological contexts this modification meaningfully alters signaling, protein biochemistry, and
structure—remains incomplete.

Our interest in SHP2 pY62 was driven by two independent observations that underscore its
potential significance. First, a comprehensive phosphoproteomic analysis identified SHP2 pY62
as one of the most recurrent phosphorylation events in the human proteome. Second, SHP2 pY62
is one of the most differentially enriched phosphopeptides across multiple RTK-driven tumor types
in patient samples. This set of observations in normal cells and tissues, cancer cells, and patient
samples prompted us to investigate the functional, mechanistic, and therapeutic consequences
of SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation.

Here we show that SHP2 pY62 is conserved across cell and cancer types and that SRC family
kinases directly phosphorylate SHP2 at Y62, downstream of RTKs. We also show that SHP2Y62D
enforces an open, active conformation, resulting in constitutive phosphatase activation that is
sufficient to activate MAPK signaling and confer resistance to allosteric SHP2 inhibitors.

---

## Results

SHP2 pY62 is a hotspot phosphorylation in normal cells/tissues and cancer cells and is
enriched in diverse RTK-driven tumor types

Inspired by cancer genomics efforts to define frequent “mutational hotspots”31-33, we performed a
comprehensive analysis of the human phosphoproteome using PhosphositePlus34. We identified
239,530 human proteins phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) across normal cells and tissues,
and cancer cells (Fig. 1b) (Supplementary Data 1 ). We determined the reported frequency of
every phosphosite by computing the sum of MS_LIT, the number of published studies reporting
the phosphosite, and MS_CST, the number of unpublished mass spectrometry experiments
performed and curated by Cell Signaling Technology, on PhosphoSitePlus. We posited that the
most frequent phosphosites may be enriched for functionality, and focused analysis on the top
2400 (1%) of phosphosites. In line with this assertion, many of the most frequent phosphosites
were known kinase activation loop sites including GSK3α pY279, GSK3β pY216, and ERK2
pY187 (Supplementary Data 1). We examined proteins with multiple phosphorylation sites and
found that the top differentially phosphorylated protein was not a kinase, but the protein
phosphatase SHP2 (Fig. 1c). The known SHP2 C-terminal tyrosine phosphosites Y542 and Y580
(pY542, pY580) (Fig. 1a) were abundant, but surprisingly, the most abundant SHP2 phosphosite
was the tyrosine Y62 (pY62) (Fig. 1c).

We next determined the experimental characterization frequency by comparing LT_LIT, the
number of low-throughput (LT), experimentally validated studies in PhosphositePlus
(Supplementary Data 1), with MS_LIT + MS_CST. By this metric, SHP2 pY62 was reported far
less frequently than the canonical C-terminal phosphorylation sites pY542 and pY58034 (Fig. 1d).
Despite this underrepresentation, SHP2 Y62 is evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates, down
to Xenopus (Supplementary Fig. 1). Notably, SHP2 Y62 is not conserved in the closely related
human phosphatase SHP1, where it aligns with phenylalanine 60 (F60), a non-phosphorylatable
residue. In contrast, the adjacent SHP2 Y63 is conserved and aligns with SHP1 Y61, indicating
selective evolutionary retention of the neighboring tyrosine, rather than the Y62-equivalent site.
SHP2 Y62 is located in a structured core on a loop between the βD and βE strands of the SHP2
N-terminal SH2 (nSH2) domain8. Among the 110 SH2-domain containing proteins in humans,
Y62-homologous tyrosines are present in 12 proteins, some of which are frequently
phosphorylated (Supplementary Fig. 1)35.

Protein phosphorylation can differ between cancer cell lines and tumors36. To understand the role
of SHP2 pY62 in patients, we determined its abundance and enrichment across genomically
defined human tumor types based on publicly available data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor
Analysis Consortium (CPTAC)37 and National Omics Data Encyclopedia (NODE)38. SHP2 pY62
has been reported as the single most differentially increased phosphosite in patients with EGFR-
mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), compared to their wild-type (WT) counterparts39
(Fig. 1e). In fact, SHP2 pY62 was more increased than phosphorylated EGFR itself (Fig. 1e,
Supplementary Data 2). Additionally, SHP2 pY62 was the second most differentially increased
phosphosite in patients with FGFR2-altered cholangiocarcinoma40 (Fig. 1f), and differentially
increased in CPTAC datasets in patients with EGFR-amplified head and neck squamous cell
carcinoma41, EGFRvIII-positive glioblastoma42, and EGFR-altered high grade glioma43, compared
to WT counterparts. In contrast, SHP2 pY62 was one of the most significantly decreased
phosphosites in KRAS-mutant NSCLC relative to wild-type NSCLC39 (Fig. 1g, Supplementary
Data 2). Our identification of SHP2 pY62 as one of the most frequently detected phosphosites in
the human phosphoproteome, along with its evolutionary conservation and selective retention
across orthologs and SH2 domains, and its high frequency in RTK-driven patient tumor types
suggests that Y62 phosphorylation may exert distinct conformational or functional effects that
contribute to RTK-driven oncogenesis.

SHP2 pY62 is downstream of RTKs, but Y62 is not phosphorylated by RTKs

Given the high abundance of pY62 across RTK-driven tumors, we hypothesized that RTKs signal
to and directly phosphorylate SHP2 Y62 in cells (Fig. 2a). To test this hypothesis, we developed
a phosphospecific SHP2 pY62 antibody and validated it in SHP2 knock out (KO) cells
overexpressing SHP2 and the phosphodead mutant Y62F (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). We serum-
starved U-2 OS (osteosarcoma) and BT20 (EGFR-amplified triple-negative breast cancer) cells
and exposed them to various RTK ligands (EGF, FGF1, PDGF). RTK stimulation led to RTK
phosphorylation at 5-10 minutes, with eventual detection of SHP2 pY62 much later, suggesting
SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation is downstream of RTKs (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Fig. 2c-e). However,
when we exposed RTK stimulated cells to RTK inhibitors against EGFR, FGFR, and PDGFR in
serum starved media, there was no decrease in SHP2 pY62 (Fig. 2c), showing that SHP2 Y62 is
not directly phosphorylated by RTKs.

SRC family kinases (SFKs) phosphorylate SHP2 Y62, Y542, and Y580

To determine the direct kinase for SHP2 Y62, we leveraged The Kinase Library, a recently
developed global atlas of protein kinome in vitro substrate specificities44,45, based on the peptide
primary sequence surrounding the phosphosite (Supplementary Data 3). For SHP2 pY62, RTKs
were predicted as the top candidate kinases (Fig. 3a). JAK3, a non-RTK, was also highly
predicted. However, exposure of cells to the JAK3 inhibitor tofacitinib did not alter the level of
SHP2 pY62 (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Interestingly, non-RTKs, such as SRC family kinases
(SFKs) SRC, YES1, and FYN, were in the bottom quartile with lower confidence scores. Since
inhibiting RTKs did not alter the SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation, we wanted to test if SFKs can
phosphorylate SHP2 Y62.

To test this hypothesis, we first used pharmacologic methods (Fig. 3b). Dasatinib is a multi-kinase
inhibitor that targets not only SFKs but also ABL, PDGFR, and c-KIT46 (Fig. 3b). Treatment with
dasatinib readily decreased SHP2 pY62 levels in U-2 OS cells (Fig. 3c) and HCC827 cells (EGFR-
mutant NSCLC) (Fig. 3d). Dasatinib treatment also decreased SHP2 pY542 and pY580 levels in
U-2 OS cells (Fig. 3c) but only pY542 in HCC827 cells (Fig. 3d). Since dasatinib has a wide range
of targets including SFKs, ABL, and c-KIT, we next chose the selective SFK inhibitor SU665647
which inhibits SRC, YES1, FYN, and LYN; asciminib48 which binds to the myristoyl binding pocket
and inhibits ABL; and ripretinib49, which inhibits c-KIT, to narrow down candidate kinases (Fig.
3b). Treatment of U-2 OS cells with SU6656 decreased SHP2 pY62, pY542, and pY580 but there
was no change in SHP2 phosphorylation with SU6656 in HCC827 cells (Fig. 3d). Treatment with
asciminib or ripretinib did not change SHP2 phosphorylation levels (Supplementary Fig. 3b).

The SFKs comprises 8 human kinases50, three of which–-SRC, YES1, and FYN–-are ubiquitously
expressed in all tissues. In contrast, other SFK kinases (BLK, FGR, HCK, LCK, and LYN) are
expressed in specific tissue types51. To our knowledge, there are no SFK inhibitors selective to
individual SFKs. To better deconvolute the contributions of specific SFK kinases, we tested the
SFK inhibitors saracatinib52 (SRC and ABL inhibitor), CH695375553 (YES1 inhibitor), and PP254
(FYN and LCK inhibitor) (Fig. 3b) which are more selective than dasatinib or SU6656 but less
potent. In HCC827 cells, SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation was inhibited by saracatinib, CH6953755
and PP2, and Y542 phosphorylation was altered by PP2 and saracatinib at high concentrations,
but not Y580 phosphorylation (Fig. 3e). In U-2 OS cells, SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation was inhibited
by saracatinib only at high concentrations, while Y542 and Y580 phosphorylation were inhibited
by saracatinib even at 1 µM (Supplementary Fig. 3c), but not by CH6953755 (Supplementary Fig.
3d) or PP2 (Supplementary Fig. 3e).

We further investigated the cell-type specificity of SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation. Since 1) dasatinib
decreased SHP2 pY62 levels in HCC827 and U-2 OS cells, 2) inhibitors of the non-SFK kinase
targets of dasatinib did not decrease SHP2 phosphorylation, and 3) selective SFK inhibitors
inhibited SHP2 pY62 levels in HCC827 but not in U-2 OS cells, we hypothesized that SHP2 Y62
phosphorylation is maintained by distinct SFK family members in a context-dependent manner,
and that broad SFK inhibition is required to suppress SHP2 pY62 across diverse cell types.

To test this hypothesis, we tested double and triple combinations of the SFK selective inhibitors
saracatinib, CH6953755, and PP2 in HCC827 and U-2 OS cells. Combining two drugs reduced
SHP2 pY62, pY542, and pY580 levels more than single drugs, and combining all three drugs
reduced levels more than combining two drugs (Fig. 3f, Supplementary Fig. 3f).

We also used mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from the SYF knock out mouse (SRC-/-, YES1
-/-, FYN -/-)55 as a genetic tool to test the hypothesis that SFKs phosphorylate SHP2 pY62. We
found that SHP2 pY62, pY542, and pY580 levels were inhibited compared to WT MEFs (Fig. 3g).
Thus, pharmacologic inhibition and genetic loss of the SFKs SRC, YES1, and FYN reduce SHP2
phosphorylation at Y62, Y542, and Y580.

Our initial growth factor experiments showed that SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation is downstream of
RTKs (Fig. 2b). We used our pharmacologic and genetic models to situate SFKs in RTK-SHP2
signaling. EGF-dependent SHP2 phosphorylation at Y62, Y542, and Y580 was abrogated when
U-2 OS cells were pretreated with dasatinib or SU6656 (Supplementary Fig. 3g). EGF-, FGF1-,
and PDGDF-dependent SHP2 phosphorylation at Y62 was abrogated in our SYF KO MEF models
compared to WT MEFs (Supplementary Fig. 3h-j). In contrast, SHP2 Y542 and Y580
phosphorylation were abrogated in SYF KO MEFs under FGF1 stimulation but not under EGF or
PDGF stimulation (Supplementary Fig. 3h-j).

Finally, to further validate that SFKs phosphorylate SHP2 Y62, we performed in vitro kinase
assays using bacterially purified recombinant SHP2. SRC, YES1, and FYN kinases
phosphorylated SHP2 WT at Y62 but not the Y62F phosphodead mutant (Fig. 3h). SRC, YES1,
and FYN also phosphorylated Y542 and Y580 in vitro (Fig. 3h). Together these data show that
SHP2 Y62 is a direct substrate of SFKs, and that SHP2 Y542 and Y580 can also be
phosphorylated by SFKs.

SHP2 Y62 phosphomimetic protein constitutively increases phosphatase activity

SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation has been proposed to disrupt its autoinhibited state through the
introduction of negative charge at the N-SH2/PTP interface, thereby enhancing phosphatase
activity, and this has been supported by biochemical and cellular experiments with the Y62
phosphomimetic mutants30,56,57. We corroborated these prior results by conducting Michaelis-
Menten enzyme kinetics with the Y62D mutant, which showed a 2.4-fold increase in k /K when
cat m
compared with wild-type SHP2 (Fig. 4a). Tyrosine to aspartate mutation is commonly used as a
phosphomimetic to model the effects of phosphorylation, though it may not fully recapitulate the
structural or binding consequences of a bona fide phosphotyrosine at this site. By contrast, the
Y542 and Y580 phosphorylation sites are thought to mediate intramolecular interactions with the
SHP2 SH2 domains or mediate intermolecular interactions with other SH2-containing proteins.
SH2-mediated interactions with tyrosine-phosphorylation proteins cannot be readily mimicked
using D/E substitutions, and indeed, the Y542D and Y580D mutations did not significantly impact
SHP2 activity (Fig. 4a). Furthermore, the combination of Y542D or Y580D with Y62D did not
appreciably impact the gain-of-function effect of Y62D (Fig. 4a).

When SHP2 auto-inhibition is disrupted by mutations, it becomes less responsive to activation by
phosphopeptides58. Indeed, unlike wild-type SHP2, Y62D-containing SHP2 variants could not be
activated by binding to an IRS-1-derived phosphopeptide (Fig. 4b). To further examine whether
these mutations disrupt auto-inhibition, we used differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF)
(Supplementary Fig. 4). Previous studies have shown that SHP2 variants with disrupted
autoinhibition tend to have lower melting temperatures59. Indeed, only SHP2 variants containing
the Y62D mutation, but not Y542D or Y580D, had decreased melting temperatures (Fig. 4c).
Collectively, these experiments show that the Y62D mutation disrupts SHP2 auto-inhibition and
corroborates the assertion that Y62 phosphorylation may disrupt auto-inhibition through
electrostatic effects.

SHP2 Y62D samples mixed open and closed conformations through increased exchange
in its buried nSH2 domain

Since the SHP2Y62D phosphomimetic protein exhibited increased enzymatic activity (Fig. 4a) and
decreased thermal instability (Fig. 4c), and since SHP2 oncogenic mutation propensity for an
open conformation correlates with increased catalysis and increased dynamic and solvent
exposure60,61, we hypothesized that SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation increases catalysis by enforcing
an open, dynamic conformation. We investigated this hypothesis using computational, structural,
and biophysical methods. We used AlphaFold2 to analyze conformational changes in SHP2Y62D
(Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Data 4) and compared the predicted structure to crystal
structures of SHP2WT, which adopts a closed conformation (PDB: 2SHP)8, and SHP2E76K, the only
SHP2 mutant with a crystal structure resolved in an open conformation (PDB: 6CRF)58. While
AlphaFold2 is not specifically powered for optimal structural prediction of missense mutations,
nonetheless, SHP2 Y62D was predicted to have a 22 Å root mean square deviation (RMSD) when
aligned with the WT crystal structure, but a 1.1 Å RMSD when aligned with the SHP2E76K structure
oncogenic mutant crystal structure, suggesting an open confirmation (Fig. 5a). We crystallized
the SHP2Y62D mutant and solved its structure at 2.63 Å resolution (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Table
1). The Y62D crystal structure exhibited a closed conformation, with a 0.5 Å RMSD when aligned
with the SHP2WT crystal structure (Fig. 5b).

Given the discordance between our biochemical and computational data and compared to our
structural data, we hypothesized that SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation samples both the closed and
open state conformations. To investigate the conformational state of the SHP2Y62D mutant, we
performed hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) with recently developed
peptide disambiguation and analysis tools62 comparing SHP2Y62D to SHP2WT and the SHP2
phosphomimetic mutant Y542D/Y580D. Compared to WT, SHP2Y62D exhibited increased
deuterium uptake across peptides spanning not only the nSH2 domain (where Y62 is located),
but also in the PTP domain mediated by amino acids that bind to and maintain nSH2 domain
autoinhibitory interactions (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. 6). Notably this PTP domain peptide
region (496-510) also includes S502, G503, and Q506 which bind to the nSH2 domain, are known
cancer-associated mutations61, and activate SHP2 in deep mutational scanning studies63. This
pattern is consistent with increased destabilization of the closed, autoinhibited conformation and
adoption of an open conformation relative to SHP2WT. In contrast, the Y542D/Y580D mutant
showed minimal differences in hydrogen exchange relative to WT, indicating that these
phosphomimetic substitutions do not strongly alter the conformational ensemble (Supplementary
Fig. 6). Together, these data demonstrate that the Y62D mutation promotes an open, active-like
conformation of SHP2, distinct from WT and Y542D/Y580D.

SHP2 Y62 phosphomimetic mutation activates MAPK signaling and causes resistance to
SHP2 inhibitors

Since SHP2 pY62 is enriched in RTK-driven tumors, we tested the role of SHP2 Y62
phosphorylation in cancer cells. We knocked out endogenous PTPN11/SHP2 using CRISPR-
Cas9 in BT20 and U-2 OS cells, which are frequently used to model SHP2 alterations30,58
(Supplementary Fig. 2a), and complemented this with lentiviral overexpression of SHP2WT,
aspartate and phenylalanine mutants at Y62 and Y542/Y580. Complementation with empty vector
control was not tolerated by cells, consistent with PTPN11/SHP2 loss being synthetic lethal in
RTK-driven cancer cells20. SHP2Y62D, but not SHP2Y62F, sustained maximal MAPK signaling as
measured by phosphorylated MEK (pMEK) and phosphorylated ERK (pERK) in SHP2 KO BT20
cells, suggesting that SHP2 pY62 is necessary for maximal MAPK signaling (Fig. 6a). To
delineate how upstream SFKs modulate MAPK signaling, we used our SYF KO MEF models.
SYF KO showed decreased pMEK and pERK as compared to WT MEFs (Fig. 3g).

Given the abundance of SHP2 pY62 across cancer cells and tumors, and the minimal response
rates conferred by SHP2i in the clinic, we hypothesized that SHP2 pY62 confers resistance to
SHP2i. We performed biochemical inhibition assays using purified recombinant SHP2WT and
SHP2Y62D proteins. SHP099 IC values were 0.2319 μM for WT and 1.356 μM for Y62D
50
(Supplementary Fig. 7), a statistically significant shift. These data show that the Y62D variant has
reduced sensitivity to allosteric SHP2 inhibition. We tested varied allosteric SHP2 inhibitors
including SHP099, RMC4550, and TNO155, which are based on similar scaffolds that stabilize
the SHP2 autoinhibited conformation20,64,65. SHP2 Y62 phosphorylation as modeled by SHP2Y62D
resulted in resistance to SHP099, RMC4550, and TNO155, as measured by sustained pERK
signaling, as well increased GAB1 phosphorylation which is a direct readout of SHP2 scaffolding
function66 (Fig. 6b-d).
